PAYABLE-ON-DEATH (POD) ACCOUNT DESIGNATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Acme Bank

ACCOUNT HOLDER AND P.O.D. BENEFICIARY DECLARATION
Jordan Alex Lee is the owner of the account described as checking account ending in 4321 at Acme Bank. Jordan Alex Lee intends this account to be designated as a P.O.D. (payable-on-death) account under California's Multiple-Party Accounts Law, naming Taylor Morgan as P.O.D. payee. If Casey Rivera is also named, Taylor Morgan and Casey Rivera are both named as P.O.D. payees, to take the sums on deposit in equal and undivided shares if both survive Jordan Alex Lee, unless Jordan Alex Lee instead directs Acme Bank in writing to use different shares. This declaration records Jordan Alex Lee's intended designation for Jordan Alex Lee's own planning purposes; it does not, by itself, create a legally effective P.O.D. designation. A P.O.D. designation becomes legally effective only when it is reflected in the signature card, beneficiary form, or other account agreement that Acme Bank itself uses to open or modify the account.

WHAT A P.O.D. ACCOUNT IS
California's Multiple-Party Accounts Law (Probate Code Part 2 of Division 5, commencing with § 5100) defines a "P.O.D. account" as an account payable on request to one person during that person's lifetime and, on that person's death, to one or more P.O.D. payees, or an account payable on request to two or more people during their lifetimes and, on the death of all of them, to one or more P.O.D. payees. A "P.O.D. payee" is the person designated on the account as the one to whom it becomes payable after the death of the party or parties who owned it. "P.O.D." is the statute's own abbreviation for "payable on death." California's statute treats a "Totten trust account" as a separate, distinctly defined type of account — one titled in the name of one or more parties "as trustee for" one or more named beneficiaries, rather than as a P.O.D. account naming P.O.D. payees. A P.O.D. account and a Totten trust account are often used interchangeably in everyday conversation because both let a bank or financial account pass to a named person at death without probate, but they are two separately defined account forms with different titling conventions under California law, alongside a third, unrelated category (a joint account). This information sheet addresses a P.O.D. account specifically, as designated on checking account ending in 4321 held at Acme Bank.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“P.O.D. account” means any of the following:(a) An account payable on request to one person during the person’s lifetime and on the person’s death to one or more P.O.D. payees.(b) An account payable on request to one or more persons during their lifetimes and on the death of all of them to one or more P.O.D. payees."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5140, California Probate Code, definition of “P.O.D. account” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5140.)
  "“P.O.D. payee” means a person designated on a P.O.D. account as one to whom the account is payable on request after the death of one or more persons."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5142, California Probate Code, definition of “P.O.D. payee” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5142.)
  "“Totten trust account” means an account in the name of one or more parties as trustee for one or more beneficiaries where the relationship is established by the form of the account and the deposit agreement with the financial institution and there is no subject of the trust other than the sums on deposit in the account."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 80, California Probate Code, definition of “Totten trust account” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=80.)
  "A “multiple-party account” is any of the following types of account:(a) A joint account.(b) A P.O.D. account.(c) A Totten trust account."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5132, California Probate Code, definition of “multiple-party account” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5132.)
  Known gap: This is California's Multiple-Party Accounts Law specifically. Other states that authorize a P.O.D. (payable-on-death) or Totten-trust bank account — many adapted from the Uniform Probate Code or the older Uniform TOD Security Registration Act rather than California's own multiple-party-account statute — are not assumed to define, create, or govern these accounts the same way, and this is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular account or financial institution's own paperwork. Separately, this statutory definition covers only what makes an account a "P.O.D. account" as a matter of California law once it exists; it does not itself address the mechanics of how such an account is opened or titled with a financial institution, which is covered in a separate clause of this document. § 5140, § 5142, § 80, and § 5132 are four separate statutory sections, each independently retrieved and independently verified.

HOW A P.O.D. DESIGNATION IS CREATED
A P.O.D. designation is not created by a will, a trust document, or any separate estate-planning instrument. It is created by the terms of the account itself — the signature card, passbook, contract, or other instrument establishing checking account ending in 4321 with Acme Bank. California's statute supplies model language for this purpose: for a P.O.D. account with a single party, "This account or certificate is owned by the named party. Upon the death of that party, ownership passes to the named pay-on-death payee(s)." For a P.O.D. account with more than one party (for example, two co-owners), the model language instead has ownership pass to the surviving party or parties first, and only on the death of all of them does ownership pass to the named P.O.D. payee(s). Using this exact model language is not legally required — an account is governed by California's Multiple-Party Accounts Law as long as the deposit agreement creates substantially the same relationship, whether or not the statute's own words are used verbatim.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(2) P.O.D. account with single party: “This account or certificate is owned by the named party. Upon the death of that party, ownership passes to the named pay-on-death payee(s).”(3) P.O.D. account with multiple parties: “This account or certificate is owned by the named parties. Upon the death of any of them, ownership passes to the survivor(s). Upon the death of all of them, ownership passes to the named pay-on-death payee(s).”"
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5203(a)(2)-(3), California Probate Code, statutory form language creating a P.O.D. account (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5203.)
  "Use of the form language provided in this section is not necessary to create an account that is governed by this part. If the contract of deposit creates substantially the same relationship between the parties as an account created using the form language provided in this section, this part applies to the same extent as if the form language had been used."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5203(b), California Probate Code, statutory form language not mandatory (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5203.)
  Known gap: This is California's Multiple-Party Accounts Law specifically. Other states that authorize a P.O.D. (payable-on-death) or Totten-trust bank account — many adapted from the Uniform Probate Code or the older Uniform TOD Security Registration Act rather than California's own multiple-party-account statute — are not assumed to define, create, or govern these accounts the same way, and this is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular account or financial institution's own paperwork. Both citations below are drawn from subdivisions (a) and (b) of the same statutory section, § 5203; they are treated as one source, not independent. Separately, this clause describes California's own model contract language, offered as evidence of how one state's statute frames account creation — not as a claim that every financial institution's actual signature-card wording tracks this language, or that a particular institution's own form and procedures are described here.

RIGHTS DURING THE ORIGINAL PARTY'S LIFETIME
During Jordan Alex Lee's lifetime, a P.O.D. designation gives Taylor Morgan no present right to the funds on deposit in checking account ending in 4321. As between Jordan Alex Lee and Taylor Morgan, the account belongs to Jordan Alex Lee; Taylor Morgan's status as P.O.D. payee carries no current ownership interest and no right to withdraw, and Acme Bank owes Taylor Morgan no duties regarding the account until Jordan Alex Lee's death. This is a default rule, not an absolute one — it can be overcome by clear and convincing evidence of a different intent. It is also a rule about beneficial ownership among the parties and payee, not about who has power to withdraw from the account day to day; that power is set independently by the account contract with Acme Bank.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "In the case of a P.O.D. account, the P.O.D. payee has no rights to the sums on deposit during the lifetime of any party, unless there is clear and convincing evidence of a different intent."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5301(d), California Probate Code, P.O.D. payee has no lifetime rights (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5301.)
  "The provisions of Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 5301) concerning beneficial ownership as between parties, or as between parties and P.O.D. payees or beneficiaries of multiple-party accounts, are relevant only to controversies between these persons and their creditors and other successors, and have no bearing on the power of withdrawal of these persons as determined by the terms of account contracts."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5201(a), California Probate Code, ownership rules do not govern withdrawal power (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5201.)
  Known gap: This is California's Multiple-Party Accounts Law specifically. Other states that authorize a P.O.D. (payable-on-death) or Totten-trust bank account — many adapted from the Uniform Probate Code or the older Uniform TOD Security Registration Act rather than California's own multiple-party-account statute — are not assumed to define, create, or govern these accounts the same way, and this is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular account or financial institution's own paperwork. The "clear and convincing evidence of a different intent" qualifier is part of the statute's own text, not an inference — this default is rebuttable, and this sheet does not attempt to describe what would count as sufficient evidence of a different intent in a given case. § 5301 and § 5201 are two separate statutory sections, each independently retrieved.

EFFECT AT DEATH — NO PROBATE REQUIRED
On the death of the sole party to checking account ending in 4321, or on the death of the last survivor if it has more than one party, any sums remaining on deposit belong to Taylor Morgan, if surviving, without a probate proceeding. This transfer takes effect by reason of the account contract with Acme Bank and the operation of California's Multiple-Party Accounts Law itself. The statute expressly states that a transfer of this kind is not to be treated as testamentary, and that Taylor Morgan's right to the funds is not denied, limited, or affected merely because it was not created by a writing that meets the formalities California otherwise requires for a valid will.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "If the account is a P.O.D. account:(1) On death of one of two or more parties, the rights to any sums remaining on deposit are governed by subdivision (a).(2) On death of the sole party or of the survivor of two or more parties, (A) any sums remaining on deposit belong to the P.O.D. payee or payees if surviving, or to the survivor of them if one or more die before the party,"
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5302(b)(1)-(2)(A), California Probate Code, sums on deposit belong to surviving P.O.D. payee(s) at death (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5302.)
  "Any transfers resulting from the application of Section 5302 are effective by reason of the account contracts involved and this part and are not to be considered as testamentary. The right under this part of a surviving party to a joint account, or of a beneficiary, or of a P.O.D. payee, to the sums on deposit on the death of a party to a multiple-party account shall not be denied, abridged, or affected because such right has not been created by a writing executed in accordance with the laws of this state prescribing the requirements to effect a valid testamentary disposition of property."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5304, California Probate Code, P.O.D. transfer is nontestamentary and valid without will formalities (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5304.)
  Known gap: This is California's Multiple-Party Accounts Law specifically. Other states that authorize a P.O.D. (payable-on-death) or Totten-trust bank account — many adapted from the Uniform Probate Code or the older Uniform TOD Security Registration Act rather than California's own multiple-party-account statute — are not assumed to define, create, or govern these accounts the same way, and this is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular account or financial institution's own paperwork. "No probate" describes only the mechanics of transferring this particular account to the P.O.D. payee; it is not a statement that the funds are shielded from the original party's creditors, from a surviving spouse's community property rights, or from other legal claims against the party's estate — those questions are addressed, to the extent the statute addresses them at all, in a separate clause of this document. Section 5302 also opens by making its rules "[s]ubject to Section 5040," California's rule that automatically revokes certain nonprobate transfers to a former spouse after divorce; that rule is discussed in the revocability clause of this document. § 5302 and § 5304 are two separate statutory sections, each independently retrieved.

MULTIPLE P.O.D. PAYEES AND SURVIVORSHIP
Jordan Alex Lee may name more than one P.O.D. payee on checking account ending in 4321 — for example, both Taylor Morgan and Casey Rivera. If two or more named P.O.D. payees survive Jordan Alex Lee, California's default rule is that they take the sums on deposit in equal and undivided shares; the parties can displace this default only by express terms in the account or deposit agreement providing for different shares. If a named P.O.D. payee does not survive Jordan Alex Lee, the sums pass to the P.O.D. payee or payees who do survive, not to the deceased payee's own estate or heirs. Once two or more P.O.D. payees have both survived Jordan Alex Lee and taken their respective shares, there is no further right of survivorship between them if one of them dies afterward — each payee's share becomes that payee's own separate property — unless the account or deposit agreement expressly provides for survivorship between the payees themselves.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "if two or more P.O.D. payees survive, any sums remaining on deposit belong to them in equal and undivided shares unless the terms of the account or deposit agreement expressly provide for different shares, and (C) if two or more P.O.D. payees survive, there is no right of survivorship in the event of death of a P.O.D. payee thereafter unless the terms of the account or deposit agreement  expressly provide for survivorship between them."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5302(b)(2)(B)-(C), California Probate Code, multiple P.O.D. payees take in equal shares; no further survivorship among payees (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5302.)
  Known gap: This is California's Multiple-Party Accounts Law specifically. Other states that authorize a P.O.D. (payable-on-death) or Totten-trust bank account — many adapted from the Uniform Probate Code or the older Uniform TOD Security Registration Act rather than California's own multiple-party-account statute — are not assumed to define, create, or govern these accounts the same way, and this is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular account or financial institution's own paperwork. This default — equal and undivided shares, with a surviving payee's share not passing back into a right of survivorship among the payees — is what the statute supplies when the account or deposit agreement is silent; it does not resolve disputes over what specific account or deposit-agreement language would count as "expressly providing" for different shares or for survivorship between payees. This is a single statutory subdivision (§ 5302(b)(2)(B)-(C)); no additional independent source was found for this.

REVOCABILITY, COMMUNITY PROPERTY, AND CREDITOR EXPOSURE AFTER DEATH
A P.O.D. designation is not an irrevocable trust and does not bind Jordan Alex Lee the way a completed, irrevocable gift would. During Jordan Alex Lee's lifetime, Jordan Alex Lee may change or eliminate the P.O.D. designation on checking account ending in 4321 only by closing the account and reopening it under different terms, by presenting Acme Bank with a signed modification agreement, or by following whatever modification procedure the deposit agreement itself provides; withdrawing funds also reduces Taylor Morgan's eventual interest by the amount withdrawn. California's statute does not treat a later will as a way to change a P.O.D. designation — a right of survivorship arising from a P.O.D. payee designation cannot be changed by will, so revoking or changing the designation requires acting on the account itself through Acme Bank, not through Jordan Alex Lee's other estate-planning documents. Separately, if a P.O.D. designation naming a former spouse as Taylor Morgan was made before or during a marriage that later ends in divorce or annulment, California's statute generally causes that designation to fail as to the former spouse, subject to statutory exceptions. If Jordan Alex Lee is married and checking account ending in 4321 was funded with community property, titling the account as a P.O.D. account does not by itself eliminate that community property character — the net contribution is presumed to remain community property, subject to a surviving spouse's community property rights, unless that presumption is rebutted in one of the specific ways the statute allows. California's Multiple-Party Accounts Law does not set out a scheme — comparable to the one it provides for a Transfer-on-Death Deed on real property — spelling out a P.O.D. payee's personal liability to Jordan Alex Lee's creditors after death, or a creditor's priority against the account; whether and how a deceased account holder's creditors can reach P.O.D. funds after death is not resolved by this statute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Once established, the terms of a multiple-party account can be changed only by any of the following methods:(1) Closing the account and reopening it under different terms.(2) Presenting to the financial institution a modification agreement that is signed by all parties with a present right of withdrawal. If the financial institution has a form for this purpose, it may require use of the form.(3) If the provisions of the terms of the account or deposit agreement provide a method of modification of the terms of the account, complying with those provisions."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5303(b)(1)-(3), California Probate Code, methods of changing the terms of a multiple-party account (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5303.)
  "Withdrawal of funds from the account by a party also eliminates rights of survivorship with respect to the funds withdrawn to the extent of the withdrawing party’s net contribution to the account."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5303(c), California Probate Code, withdrawal reduces survivorship rights (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5303.)
  "A right of survivorship arising from the express terms of the account or under this section, a beneficiary designation in a Totten trust account, or a P.O.D. payee designation, cannot be changed by will."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5302(e), California Probate Code, P.O.D. designation cannot be changed by will (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5302.)
  "Notwithstanding Sections 5301 to 5303, inclusive, if parties to an account are married to each other, whether or not they are so described in the deposit agreement, their net contribution to the account is presumed to be and remain their community property."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5305(a), California Probate Code, community property presumption for married parties' account (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5305.)
  "a nonprobate transfer to the transferor’s former spouse, in an instrument executed by the transferor before or during the marriage or registered domestic partnership, fails if, at the time of the transferor’s death, the former spouse is not the transferor’s surviving spouse"
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5040(a), California Probate Code, nonprobate transfer to former spouse fails after divorce (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5040.)
  Known gap: This is California's Multiple-Party Accounts Law specifically. Other states that authorize a P.O.D. (payable-on-death) or Totten-trust bank account — many adapted from the Uniform Probate Code or the older Uniform TOD Security Registration Act rather than California's own multiple-party-account statute — are not assumed to define, create, or govern these accounts the same way, and this is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular account or financial institution's own paperwork. The two § 5303 citations below (subdivisions (b) and (c)) are drawn from the same statutory section and are treated as one source, not independent; § 5302(e), § 5305, and § 5040 are three further, separate statutory sections, each independently retrieved and verified. The statute never uses the word "revocable" to describe a P.O.D. account the way it does for a Transfer-on-Death Deed — revocability here is this sheet's own accurate description of what the modification mechanics in § 5303 actually permit, not a quotation of a labeled "revocability" provision. On creditor exposure specifically: this sheet discloses honestly that no comparable statutory scheme was located within the Multiple-Party Accounts Law itself; the absence of such a provision is not the same as an affirmative statutory statement that P.O.D. funds are immune from creditor claims, and a reader should not assume either outcome from this silence.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
SIGNATURE AND DATE: Jordan Alex Lee signs and dates this declaration below.

Signature of Jordan Alex Lee: _________________________ Date: _______________

Printed name: _________________________

ACKNOWLEDGMENT: Jordan Alex Lee understands that this declaration is a planning worksheet reflecting Jordan Alex Lee's intended P.O.D. designation for checking account ending in 4321 at Acme Bank, and that it does not itself open, modify, or bind any account. Jordan Alex Lee understands that to make the designation legally effective, Jordan Alex Lee must separately complete Acme Bank's own signature card, beneficiary form, or account agreement naming Taylor Morgan (and Casey Rivera, if applicable) as P.O.D. payee, and that Acme Bank may require government-issued identification, an original signature, or additional paperwork of its own choosing before doing so. Jordan Alex Lee further understands that the designation can generally be changed or revoked during Jordan Alex Lee's lifetime only by acting on the account itself through Acme Bank — for example by closing and reopening the account, or by signing a modification agreement — and not by a later will alone.

NOTARIZATION NOTICE: California's Multiple-Party Accounts Law does not require this declaration to be notarized or witnessed to be effective; what governs is the account or deposit agreement actually on file with Acme Bank. This declaration is kept for Jordan Alex Lee's own records, alongside a copy of the P.O.D. paperwork Acme Bank provides.

expectedJSON.body: Jordan Alex Lee may name more than one P.O.D. payee on checking account ending in 4321 — for example, both Taylor Morgan and Casey Rivera. If two or more named P.O.D. payees survive Jordan Alex Lee, California's default rule is that they take the sums on deposit in equal and undivided shares; the parties can displace this default only by express terms in the account or deposit agreement providing for different shares. If a named P.O.D. payee does not survive Jordan Alex Lee, the sums pass to the P.O.D. payee or payees who do survive, not to the deceased payee's own estate or heirs. Once two or more P.O.D. payees have both survived Jordan Alex Lee and taken their respective shares, there is no further right of survivorship between them if one of them dies afterward — each payee's share becomes that payee's own separate property — unless the account or deposit agreement expressly provides for survivorship between the payees themselves.

expectedJSON.body: A P.O.D. designation is not an irrevocable trust and does not bind Jordan Alex Lee the way a completed, irrevocable gift would. During Jordan Alex Lee's lifetime, Jordan Alex Lee may change or eliminate the P.O.D. designation on checking account ending in 4321 only by closing the account and reopening it under different terms, by presenting Acme Bank with a signed modification agreement, or by following whatever modification procedure the deposit agreement itself provides; withdrawing funds also reduces Taylor Morgan's eventual interest by the amount withdrawn. California's statute does not treat a later will as a way to change a P.O.D. designation — a right of survivorship arising from a P.O.D. payee designation cannot be changed by will, so revoking or changing the designation requires acting on the account itself through Acme Bank, not through Jordan Alex Lee's other estate-planning documents. Separately, if a P.O.D. designation naming a former spouse as Taylor Morgan was made before or during a marriage that later ends in divorce or annulment, California's statute generally causes that designation to fail as to the former spouse, subject to statutory exceptions. If Jordan Alex Lee is married and checking account ending in 4321 was funded with community property, titling the account as a P.O.D. account does not by itself eliminate that community property character — the net contribution is presumed to remain community property, subject to a surviving spouse's community property rights, unless that presumption is rebutted in one of the specific ways the statute allows. California's Multiple-Party Accounts Law does not set out a scheme — comparable to the one it provides for a Transfer-on-Death Deed on real property — spelling out a P.O.D. payee's personal liability to Jordan Alex Lee's creditors after death, or a creditor's priority against the account; whether and how a deceased account holder's creditors can reach P.O.D. funds after death is not resolved by this statute.

citations.cite: California Probate Code, methods of changing the terms of a multiple-party account
citations.quote: Once established, the terms of a multiple-party account can be changed only by any of the following methods:(1) Closing the account and reopening it under different terms.(2) Presenting to the financial institution a modification agreement that is signed by all parties with a present right of withdrawal. If the financial institution has a form for this purpose, it may require use of the form.(3) If the provisions of the terms of the account or deposit agreement provide a method of modification of the terms of the account, complying with those provisions.

citations.cite: California Probate Code, withdrawal reduces survivorship rights
citations.quote: Withdrawal of funds from the account by a party also eliminates rights of survivorship with respect to the funds withdrawn to the extent of the withdrawing party’s net contribution to the account.

citations.cite: California Probate Code, P.O.D. designation cannot be changed by will
citations.quote: A right of survivorship arising from the express terms of the account or under this section, a beneficiary designation in a Totten trust account, or a P.O.D. payee designation, cannot be changed by will.

citations.cite: California Probate Code, community property presumption for married parties' account
citations.quote: Notwithstanding Sections 5301 to 5303, inclusive, if parties to an account are married to each other, whether or not they are so described in the deposit agreement, their net contribution to the account is presumed to be and remain their community property.

citations.cite: California Probate Code, nonprobate transfer to former spouse fails after divorce
citations.quote: a nonprobate transfer to the transferor’s former spouse, in an instrument executed by the transferor before or during the marriage or registered domestic partnership, fails if, at the time of the transferor’s death, the former spouse is not the transferor’s surviving spouse
